claim: Single robotic parcel induction/singulation benchmarks cluster around 1,500-1,800 pph, while smaller robot sort cells can be closer to 325-400 pph.
context: Use as an unreviewed adjacent benchmark for the v0 suction-arm cell. Sustained throughput will depend on induction spacing, robot cycle time, suction success, barcode/OCR read rate, and downstream conveyor/WCS acceptance.

claim: Adjacent robotic parcel systems report roughly 98-99.5% picking, singulation, barcode-read, or correct-output accuracy.
context: These are not identical measures. Product-level sort accuracy should eventually split no-read, no-pick, double-pick, wrong-destination, and manual-correction rates.

claim: Adjacent robotic parcel systems span very light mailers through parcels up to 35 kg, while the v0 target remains 0.05-25 kg.
context: The active product boundary uses vacuum suction; packaging material, suction cup geometry, acceleration, and robot payload will narrow the practical field range.

claim: Adjacent robotic parcel systems report envelopes from small mailers to parcels as large as 70 x 70 x 120 cm; the v0 target keeps the longest dimension at about 700 mm.
context: Field limits depend on camera field of view, suction reach, conveyor spacing, and irregular soft-pack behavior rather than dimensions alone.

claim: Public vendor claims give proxy exception rates such as failed grasp, double-parcel grasp, and uptime, but do not yet provide a reviewed site-level jam rate for the v0 cell.
context: Treat the metric as an exception-risk order of magnitude. A proper jam metric needs field logs across failed pick, double pick, no-read, chute jam, conveyor jam, and stop/recovery events.

claim: Manual intervention is currently estimated from adjacent no-read, failed-grasp, in-size sortability, and uptime proxies rather than direct field intervention logs.
context: This remains a weak investor-facing metric. Replace with shift-level exception and labor logs before treating it as established.

claim: Adjacent pre-engineered robotic parcel stations advertise same-day readiness to under-one-week integration, but site-specific commissioning can dominate.
context: Brownfield conveyor geometry, guarding, WCS/PLC interface, compressed air, electrical work, and acceptance testing can make installation much longer than module-level claims.

claim: Annual maintenance for the 300,000 RMB parcel sorting robot cell is modeled at p50 24,000 RMB/year with a 12,000-45,000 RMB/year proxy range.
context: Low-confidence benchmark, not a field quote. The range applies 4-15% annual maintenance heuristics from industrial robot and adjacent equipment sources to the 300,000 RMB replacement value, then adds parcel-cell scope assumptions for robot PM, EOAT wear, conveyor/sensor work, and calibration. It excludes downtime opportunity cost, major overhaul, and WCS subscription/support unless separately quoted.

claim: Broader parcel sortation automation guides often frame payback around 24-48 months, but the 300,000 RMB cell needs a site-specific ROI model.
context: Payback depends on labor rates, shift count, parcel volume, throughput actually achieved, exception rate, maintenance cost, and whether the cell avoids larger conveyor-sorter capex.

claim: Low-cost conveyor integration requires stable induction and spacing control; otherwise parcel timing and presentation drive jams, no-reads, and robot intervention misses.
Barcode/OCR reading requires label localization before decoding or text recognition can be applied reliably.
context: Software decomposition backfill for the parcel-sorting cell; label-region detection is separated from decoder/OCR runtime because glare, skew, occlusion, and multiple labels can fail earlier in the pipeline.

claim: Barcode/OCR reading requires an industrial barcode decoding runtime for 1D and 2D parcel codes.
context: Software decomposition backfill; candidate suppliers advertise fixed readers, code readers, and scanning systems for logistics, but target-cell supplier status is not verified.

claim: Barcode/OCR reading requires a separate OCR runtime when parcel label text must be read as a fallback or routing token.
context: Software decomposition backfill; OCR behavior is distinct from barcode decoding and depends on label typography, image quality, and benchmark coverage.

claim: Barcode/OCR reading requires explicit no-read recovery so unread parcels do not silently become manual exceptions.
context: Software decomposition backfill; failed reads need retry, diagnostics, confidence thresholds, WCS exception routing, and manual-keying handoff.

claim: Barcode/OCR reading requires parcel-label image and annotation data to tune localization, OCR, no-read handling, and benchmark coverage.
context: Software/data decomposition backfill. Dataset scope remains unreviewed and should be split further once project-specific parcel, lighting, and label conditions are known.

claim: Barcode/OCR reading requires benchmark metrics for read rate, no-read rate, false reads, latency, and exception rate under parcel-cell conditions.
context: Benchmark decomposition backfill. This makes gate gaps explicit instead of substituting vendor product claims for measured field performance.

claim: PLC/WCS integration maturity is constrained by the software-and-controls handshake and fault-recovery loop, not only by electronics availability.
Vision processing compute maturity depends on real-time low-cost compute integration, SDK/runtime coupling, thermal design, and latency control.
Vision processing compute requires an industrial edge-AI computer or equivalent embedded compute module suitable for parcel vision workloads.
context: Hardware decomposition backfill; exact form factor may be an industrial PC, embedded Jetson/Intel edge box, or compute-integrated smart camera.

claim: Low-cost real-time vision compute integration requires model deployment optimization to meet latency and memory limits on edge hardware.
context: Software integration decomposition; separate from model accuracy and camera hardware.

claim: Low-cost real-time vision compute integration requires a pinned inference runtime stack for the selected edge hardware.
context: Runtime decomposition; includes vendor runtime libraries and deployment packaging rather than a model-training system.

claim: Low-cost real-time vision compute integration requires a stable camera SDK and frame-acquisition pipeline.
context: Camera I/O decomposition; dropped frames, buffering, trigger timing, and SDK coupling are modeled separately from camera hardware.

claim: Low-cost real-time vision compute integration requires an end-to-end latency and timestamping budget aligned to conveyor and robot timing.
context: Timing decomposition; a lab-fast model can still fail if image timestamps, inference latency, and actuation windows are not aligned.

claim: Low-cost real-time vision compute integration requires thermal management so the edge-AI computer does not throttle or fail in a sorting-cell environment.
context: Deployment decomposition; thermal risk is separated because low-cost hardware can benchmark well in lab conditions but derate in a dusty, warm conveyor cell.

claim: Robot base maturity depends on repeatable installation, alignment, anchoring, vibration checking, and commissioning, not only on steel availability.
Suction cup array maturity depends on contact qualification across variable parcel surfaces, not only elastomer feedstock availability.
Vacuum valve and blow-off maturity depends on dynamic timing, contamination tolerance, leakage handling, and robot-motion synchronization.
